clue.text: Where hammer falls promptly

definitions.meaning: a hammer is meant to strike the head of a nail, so that is where its blow lands
paying on the spot, without any delay

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally places the hammer blow, and idiomatically means paying immediately, a sense from traders settling cash at once.

clue.text: Away on holiday, achieved delivery

parts.note: away means off, as in 'off work'
a holiday is a break

explanation.surface: Someone gets a parcel delivered successfully while away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an off-break is a ball bowled to turn from the off side, so 'delivery' is the bowler's ball, not a parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket every ball the bowler sends down is a delivery, and this spinning ball is one kind.

clue.text: Food and drink

definitions.meaning: grilled bread is a simple food
to drink someone's health raising glasses

explanation.definitionFit: Toasted bread is food, and raising a glass in tribute is drinking a toast.

clue.text: Caught up in net, dangle, squirming

indicators.note: squirming describes wriggling about, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A creature dangling in a net squirms, trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squirming' shuffles the letters of NET and DANGLE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tangled in something means being caught up in it.

clue.text: Satisfy animal, stuffing it with vegetables

indicators.note: stuffing the animal with something means filling it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: an ape is an animal
peas are vegetables

explanation.surface: Keep a pet happy by feeding it a load of vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' being stuffed is the animal itself, so the vegetables go inside it, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To placate someone is to satisfy their demands.

clue.text: Bill, a mischievous creature, climbing into water channel

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a leat is a channel bringing water to a mill

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the word reads upwards, so it is turned backwards

parts.note: an elf is a mischievous little creature

explanation.surface: A man called Bill watches an imp clamber into a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: A leat is a millstream, a word mostly known from crosswords; in a down clue 'climbing' reads the creature from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a printed notice handed out, much like a flyer.

clue.text: To catch girl, ring is needed

parts.note: a lass is a girl
the letter O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone wanting to win a girl needs an engagement ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To catch' is a verb phrase and the answer is used as a verb, to rope an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy ropes cattle with a looped rope, a way of catching them.

clue.text: Milky fluid from past times

parts.note: late means former or past, as in the late president
X is the multiplication sign for times

explanation.surface: A milky liquid comes down to us from long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubber trees exude a white milky sap used to make rubber.

clue.text: After wine, clergymen used to show penitence

indicators.note: after says the clergymen come behind the wine in the answer

parts.note: sack is an old word for a dry white wine, like sherry
the cloth means the clergy collectively

explanation.surface: Clergy hit the wine, then had to show remorse.
explanation.walkthrough: SACK is an old name for sherry-like wine; 'the cloth' is the clergy as a body.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough sacking was worn, often with ashes, as a sign of repentance and mourning.

clue.text: Pupil no longer has desire for geometric construction

parts.note: a former pupil is an old boy, abbreviated OB
to long is to desire

explanation.surface: A former student still yearns for geometry lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: OB is old boy, a former pupil of a British school.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle longer than it is wide is a geometric figure.

clue.text: Fine point producing blow-out

parts.note: F is the pencil-lead abbreviation for fine
east is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A neat detail leads to a burst tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow-out is slang for a huge meal, a banquet.

clue.text: Fish around to catch by hand — that's said to be "hands-on"

indicators.note: around tells us the fish name is turned back to front

parts.note: a carp is a fish

indicators.note: said to be marks the ending as how a word sounds when spoken

parts.note: tickling trout is catching them by hand in a stream

explanation.surface: Catching a fish by hand is called a truly hands-on method.
explanation.walkthrough: Tickling trout means stroking a fish in the water until it can be lifted out by hand, so the phrase is a real catching method, not a whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: A hands-on approach is practical, involving direct doing rather than theory.

clue.text: Pierrot undaunted, to some extent, in impressive hall

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A fearless clown performs in a grand hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A round domed building or hall is an imposing piece of architecture.

clue.text: Dictionary study in pursuit of old word for "law'

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Dictionary study in pursuit of old word for "law'': CON after LEX gives LEXCON; nothing supplies the I, so a word (likely 'one') seems lost in OCR, and no search found the printed clue.
annotationWithheld.clue: Dictionary study in pursuit of old word for "law'

clue.text: A cold part of London — not a leg to be seen — just part of one

parts.note: a chill is a cold

indicators.note: not says the following letter is left out of the area name

parts.note: the East End is the eastern part of London
the leg side in cricket is also called the on side

explanation.surface: A Londoner's chilly district, with not a leg in sight, is only half seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' removes an A from EAST END, a district of London, giving ESTEND; 'leg' is ON, the cricket field's on side. 'one' refers back to the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: This tendon links the calf to the heel, a piece of the leg's anatomy.

clue.text: Rain's held off — bad luck!

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The rain has stopped at last, yet the speaker grumbles about misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges RAINSHELD. HARD LINES is a British exclamation of sympathy.
explanation.definitionFit: A British exclamation of sympathy, like 'tough luck!'.

clue.text: One carping, having a pound, keeping it quiet

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the other letters sit within

parts.note: a nicker is British slang for a pound sterling
taken as written
p, piano, means quiet in music

explanation.surface: A complainer with a pound in pocket keeps it hush-hush.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicker is British slang for a pound sterling; 'keeping' wraps it round the two pieces, which go in just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fussing over trivial faults is a constant complainer.

clue.text: Distracted if centre is out of position

indicators.note: letters out of position have been displaced and rearranged

explanation.surface: A footballer is distracted because the centre is out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of position' shuffles IFCENTRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Frantic and wildly agitated, the sense of being driven to distraction.

clue.text: Of course declarer's upset about this much older partner

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumbled letters enclose the slang
upset means knocked over, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: natch is slang short for naturally, meaning of course

explanation.surface: A bridge declarer is naturally annoyed by a much older partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' is not filler: natch, short for naturally, is the piece the shuffled declarer's letters go round. The bridge picture of a declarer hides the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dating a far younger person is jokingly said to be stealing from the nursery.

clue.text: Pleasingly simple lament cut short by worker

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: an elegy is a lament
the ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: A mournful song, trimmed back, is made stylish by a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the Y from ELEGY.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegant often means neat and graceful in its simplicity, like an elegant proof.

clue.text: Close match, in which one retires

parts.note: nigh means near or close
a tie is a match or fixture, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: In a tight game, a player retires injured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retires' means going to bed, not leaving the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightdress is worn when going to bed, retiring for the night.

clue.text: Warning signal — has to be a trick

parts.note: a con is a trick or swindle

explanation.surface: An alarm turns out to be a hoax.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire lit on a hill to warn of danger is a signal.

clue.text: Speeds between points in darkness

indicators.note: between says one piece sits inside the pair

parts.note: E for east, twice, gives two compass points
clips means speeds, as in going at a fair clip

explanation.surface: Someone races between dots on a map in the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'between' puts CLIPS inside E and E.
explanation.definitionFit: When the moon blocks the sun, daylight gives way to an eerie dimness.

clue.text: Professional co-ordinates authorisation for agent

parts.note: pro is short for professional
x and y are the usual names of graph co-ordinates

explanation.surface: A professional arranges the paperwork for an agent.
explanation.definitionFit: A proxy is the authority given to someone to act or vote on your behalf.

clue.text: Dog seen to bare teeth without backing off

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside says one piece goes round the other

parts.note: to grin is to bare the teeth

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word off is turned around

explanation.surface: A dog snarls but then backs away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, as in the hymn's 'green hill far away, without a city wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: The griffon is a breed of small wiry-coated dog.

clue.text: Runs into vessel's bow

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a font is a vessel for holy water in church
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone rushes onto the prow of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts R inside FONT, the church's baptismal vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The bow of a ship is its fore part.

clue.text: In agreement with letter? Not I. for one

definitions.meaning: being in harmony or accord with something
a letter that is not a vowel, such as I

explanation.definitionFit: The word means harmonious with, and also names any letter other than a vowel, so not I.

clue.text: As form of punishment, king has knight dismissed

parts.note: K is king in chess notation
N is knight in chess notation
a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: A king punishes by sending a knight away.
explanation.walkthrough: A knout is a Russian whip used for flogging.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian whip used for flogging criminals.

clue.text: No way in — that's bad

indicators.note: in says the way sits inside the word for no

parts.note: nay means no
St is street, a way

explanation.surface: No entry: that's unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No way in' reads like a sign barring entry; really it is two pieces and a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nasty is unpleasant or bad.

clue.text: Not 10 to three, roughly one to 100

indicators.note: roughly means approximately arranged, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: Odds are given as somewhere near three-to-one or a hundred-to-one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not 10' points to 10-across: the answer is the opposite of practical. 'roughly' shuffles TOTHREE into THEORET.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstract theory is the opposite of practical application.
